stories.title: Chicago/Midwest People & Company News, week of August 21, 2026
stories.excerpt: McColly Bennett Commercial Advantage is expanding its commercial real estate brokerage and dealmaking presence in Will County, establishing an office and adding two brokers in New Lenox. The firm has named Joe Nugent a vice president and real estate broker, and Esmerelda Roman a real estate broker. With this commercial focus in New Lenox, McColly Bennett Commercial Advantage now has a presence in Valparaiso, Dyer, Bourbonnais and New Lenox. Cleveland-based KeyBank Real Estate Capital announced that Brandon David has joined the organization as a vice president within its income property group. David reports to Robert Ray, the group’s regional executive, and will be responsible for managing and expanding relationships with West Coast-based real estate sponsors across all product types. He works closely with clients to deliver a broad range of financing solutions, including construction and bridge financing, permanent debt, agency lending, and balance sheet execution. RMK Management Corp. has been hired to oversee leasing and property management for The Bellwether, a 14-story, 117-unit rental community in Chicago’s Loop neighborhood that is the office-to-residential conversion of the former office building at 79 W. Monroe. Originally built in 1905, the property underwent a major expansion in 1924 and has served as office space and as a major bank headquarters. In 2025, R2 Companies began the redevelopment of the landmark structure. It is the first office-to-residential conversion to be completed as part of the city of Chicago’s LaSalle Street revitalization initiative. Devon Self Storage, a member of The Inland Real Estate Group of Companies, Inc., has assumed property management for three self-storage facilities in Harrisonburg, Virginia, and Bowling Green, Kentucky, further expanding the company’s third-party management platform across key regional markets. bullets: McColly Bennett Commercial Advantage expanded to Will County, New Lenox with two new brokers.
KeyBank Real Estate Capital hired VP Brandon David for West Coast construction/permanent multifamily lending.
RMK Management hired to lease/manage The Bellwether, 117-unit office-to-residential conversion Loop Chicago.
stories.summary: McColly Bennett Commercial Advantage opened a New Lenox office in Will County with two new brokers, bolstering commercial brokerage presence across four Illinois suburbs. KeyBank Real Estate Capital added VP Brandon David to expand construction and permanent financing relationships with West Coast multifamily sponsors. Meanwhile, RMK Management was hired to lease and manage The Bellwether, a 117-unit office-to-residential conversion at 79 W. Monroe in Chicago's Loop.
stories.impact: Brokerage expansion in Will County (exurban Chicago) and KeyBank's West Coast lending push suggest activity in suburban and tertiary markets; office-to-residential conversions in Loop signal capital chasing conversion opportunities in softening office markets, not ground-up apartment demand growth. Watch Loop conversion velocities—bulk of demand likely from capital recycling, not net new renters.

stories.title: Interra Realty Brokers Edgewater Apartment Transaction
stories.excerpt: Interra Realty brokered the $2.135 million sale of 1433 W. Ardmore Ave., a 13-unit multifamily building in Chicago’s Edgewater neighborhood. The transaction equates to $164,230 per unit. Interra Director Joe Braun represented the private seller. Interra Associate Tommy Richard represented the undisclosed local buyer. This is the first time the asset has traded hands in nearly 50 years. “This transaction is a good example of the enduring demand we’re seeing for value-add opportunities in Chicago, particularly those assets where an extensive repositioning can unlock additional value,” said Richard. Originally constructed in 1927, the building includes 10 one-bedroom and three two-bedroom layouts. The buyer plans a full gut rehab of the property, which is currently less than half occupied, including reconfiguring the existing units and adding new ones. Located less than a mile from Kathy Osterman Beach, 1433 W. Ardmore is close to dining and shopping offerings along Clark Street. Where the apartment industry connects. Meet the owners, investors, developers, lenders, brokers, and service providers driving today’s multifamily market at Connect Apartments. Build relationships, uncover opportunities, and stay ahead of what’s next. The post Interra Realty Brokers Edgewater Apartment Transaction appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Interra Realty brokered $2.135M sale of 13-unit Edgewater building at $164,230/unit.
1927 construction, first trade in 50 years; currently <50% occupied, buyer plans full gut rehab.
Local buyer unlocking value through repositioning in tight Edgewater supply.
stories.summary: Interra Realty closed the sale of 1433 W. Ardmore Ave., a 13-unit multifamily building in Chicago's Edgewater, for $2.135 million ($164,230/unit). The 1927-built asset traded for the first time in nearly 50 years. The undisclosed local buyer plans a full gut rehab with unit reconfiguration and potential unit addition to restore the property from below 50% occupancy. The building is proximate to Kathy Osterman Beach and Clark Street retail/dining.
stories.impact: Value-add repositioning in Edgewater (strong demand submarket near lakefront and transit) signals sustained investor appetite for older, underutilized assets. Low occupancy + proven demographic demand makes this a recoverable play; extrapolate to similar vintage Edgewater/Lakeview inventory for near-term acquisition and reposition opportunities before rents spike.

stories.title: Lee & Associates of Illinois Brokers Two Orland Park Property Sales
stories.excerpt: Lee & Associates has closed a pair of sale transactions in Orland Park, Illinois. Carole Caveney, senior vice president at Lee & Associates’ Illinois office, represented the seller, Marquette Bank, on the off-market disposition of a 10,892-square-foot office building at 15959 S. 108th Avenue in Orland Park, Illinois. John Arends of Colliers represented the buyer, a private investor. The one-story building is situated on a 1.45-acre lot that features 61 parking spaces. Caveney also represented the buyer, Vision Land, LLC, on the purchase of a 13.3-acre retail land site at the southwest corner of 183rd Street and LaGrange Road in Orland Park. The buyer is in the process of updating the survey and early planning for a mixed-use commercial pad site. Chris Condon of John Greene Commercial represented the seller, Synergy Property Holdings. The post Lee & Associates of Illinois Brokers Two Orland Park Property Sales appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Lee & Associates closed two Orland Park transactions: 10,892 SF office sale and 13.3-acre retail land purchase.
Office building (15959 S. 108th Ave) sold as off-market disposition; retail land buyer Vision LLC planning mixed-use pad site.
Orland Park suburban market shifting from pure office to mixed-use development.
stories.summary: Lee & Associates brokered two off-market transactions in Orland Park, Illinois. Marquette Bank sold a one-story, 10,892-square-foot office building on 1.45 acres at 15959 S. 108th Avenue. Separately, Vision Land LLC purchased 13.3 acres at 183rd Street and LaGrange Road for mixed-use commercial pad site development. Both deals reflect suburban Cook County repositioning.
stories.impact: Office disposition in exurban Orland Park (southwest Chicago metro) coupled with retail/mixed-use land acquisition signals shift away from pure office in suburban submarkets. Mixed-use pads often include multifamily; monitor Vision LLC's plans for retail/apartment split—if multifamily anchors the pad, this marks downstream demand pressure and potential site competitive for regional developers.

stories.title: L.A. County Investment Sales Jump 28% in July Thanks to Multifamily
stories.excerpt: Commercial real estate investment sales accelerated across Los Angeles County in July, with multifamily accounting for the majority of capital deployed. About 7.25 million square feet of commercial property traded for $2.1 billion last month, NAI Capital reported Thursday, citing CoStar data. Compared to July 2025, almost 22 percent more square footage traded hands during July to make for a 28.5 percent jump in dollar volume. Compared with July 2024, sales volume climbed 75 percent. The gains came despite elevated borrowing costs, with long-term Treasury yields remaining near multiyear highs. Multifamily dominated, with 3.43 million square feet changing hands for $1.22 billion — accounting for 58 percent of all investment during the month in L.A. County. Sales volume increased 55 percent since last year, and almost 166 percent compared to July 2024. Average pricing rose 28.7 percent to $376 per square foot. People look at the Los Angeles skyline from Griffith Observatory. PHOTO: Matt McNulty - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images Retail also posted broad gains. About 1.23 million square feet sold for $402 million, pushing dollar volume up 40 percent from a year ago, and nearly doubling the July 2024 total. Retail square footage traded has climbed 135 percent over the same two-year period. Industrial faces a more complicated environment. About 1.33 million square feet traded in July, which is almost 71 percent higher since 2025, but dollar volume remained about flat at $214 million, and average pricing fell 3.6 percent to $273 per square foot. Office was the only major property type to decline in both sales volume and square footage. About 1.26 million square feet sold for $262 million, down 9.7 percent and 23.4 percent, respectively, from July 2025. Average pricing dropped 23.5 percent to $250 per square foot. bullets: L.A. County investment sales rose 28.5% YoY in July 2026 to $2.1B; multifamily drove 58% of volume.
Multifamily sales jumped 55% YoY and 166% YoY (vs. July 2024); avg. price $376/SF (up 28.7%).
Gains despite elevated long-term Treasury yields near multiyear highs.
stories.summary: Los Angeles County commercial real estate investment sales accelerated in July 2026, with 7.25 million square feet trading for $2.1 billion—a 28.5% dollar increase YoY. Multifamily dominated, accounting for 58% of capital deployed: 3.43 million SF sold for $1.22 billion, up 55% YoY and 166% since July 2024. Average multifamily pricing rose 28.7% to $376/SF. Investment appetite remained strong despite elevated long-term Treasury yields.
stories.impact: L.A. County multifamily sales velocity and pricing growth (28.7% increase) signal strong investor capital despite high rates; suggests stable or rising rents underwriting deal returns. Developers should accelerate land acquisition and entitlements in L.A. submarkets before pricing locks in; cap rate compression is driven by capital supply, not rental demand softening. Monitor July-August 2026 lease-up and rent growth for sign of sustained demand.

stories.title: CBRE Arranges Sale of Boutique Bergen County Apartments
stories.excerpt: A CBRE team led by Jeffrey Dunne, Stuart MacKenzie, Eric Apfel, Travis Langer and Eric Greenberg of CBRE Institutional Properties, in partnership with Charles Berger of CBRE Investment Properties, closed the sale of Lexington Riverview, a Class A multifamily property located in the Bergen County community of Fair Lawn, NJ, for $14.9 million. CBRE represented the seller while David Ferber with Matthews represented the buyer. Completed in 2021, Lexington Riverview is a boutique luxury apartment community consisting of 43 market-rate apartments. The property is situated along the Passaic River, offering waterfront views, while only a mile away from NJ Transit’s Radburn Train Station, providing daily access to New York in approximately 45 minutes. “We generated significant interest in the asset by combining CBRE’s institutional and private capital platforms,” said Berger. “We’re thrilled with the outcome, especially given the challenges in today’s market driven by interest rate volatility.” The post CBRE Arranges Sale of Boutique Bergen County Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CBRE arranged $14.9M sale of Lexington Riverview, 43-unit Class A luxury in Fair Lawn, NJ.
2021-built boutique community; buyer (Matthews rep) acquired at strong price despite 'interest rate volatility.'
Location: Passaic River waterfront, 1 mile to NJ Transit Radburn Station (45 min to NYC).
stories.summary: CBRE Institutional Properties closed the sale of Lexington Riverview, a 43-unit Class A luxury multifamily property in Bergen County's Fair Lawn, NJ, for $14.9 million. The 2021-built boutique community sits along the Passaic River with waterfront views and proximity to NJ Transit's Radburn Train Station, providing ~45-minute access to New York City. CBRE represented the seller and attributed interest generation to institutional and private capital platforms.
stories.impact: Bergen County luxury multifamily (transit-proximate, NYC-commutable) remained liquid despite 'interest rate volatility,' per buyer rep—signals strong demand from NYC metro white-collar inbound migration. Fair Lawn/Bergen County represents secondary market opportunity for transit-oriented luxury development; renters priced out of Manhattan/Hudson County are leaking into NJ suburbs. Aquire transit-adjacent sites in Bergen/Passaic corridor before pricing spikes.

stories.title: New York City’s Technology Labor Market Has Surpassed San Francisco: Report
stories.excerpt: It’s official. New York is employing more tech workers than the San Francisco Bay area. According to an annual CBRE report on North American tech talent, the New York metropolitan area’s tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025. The stat marks an 8.4 percent increase from 2022 that added 30,640 jobs. Meanwhile, San Francisco’s tech employment fell by 6 percent over the same period, totaling 375,730 jobs in 2025. This is the first time in the report’s 13-year history that the Big Apple has come out ahead. The city’s diversified job market helped set it apart, Colin Yasukochi, executive director of CBRE’s tech insights center, told Commercial Observer. “What really pushed New York past the San Francisco Bay Area has been the job reductions that we’ve seen [in San Francisco], with a lot of the announced layoffs, and the fact that New York has continued to grow,” Yasukochi said. San Francisco remains in North America’s top spot for its pool of tech talent, however, ranked across 13 metrics. The report, which analyzed the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and LinkedIn data, found that tech jobs make up more than 10 percent of total employment in San Francisco, compared to just 4.2 percent in New York. But a whopping 61 percent of San Francisco’s tech talent works directly in the tech industry, according to CBRE’s report, leaving its general labor market vulnerable. In New York City, just 34 percent of its tech workers work within the industry, while 21 percent work in tech roles in finance, insurance and real estate industries (otherwise known as FIRE). “[That] has given New York resilience from the tech downturn that broadly started in 2022, in terms of employment,” Yasukochi said. “But, obviously, with the artificial intelligence industry coming into play, that’s turned around quite substantially in the last year.” Yasukochi added that New York also benefits from a massive university infrastructure and lower wages than San Francisco, on average, for
bullets: NYC tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025, up 8.4% since 2022 (+30,640 jobs).
SF tech employment fell 6% over same period to 375,730; first time NYC surpasses SF in 13-year report.
NYC's diversified job market and SF layoffs drove reversal; SF still leads on talent pool depth.
stories.summary: According to CBRE's annual North American tech talent report, New York City's tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025, marking an 8.4% increase since 2022 (+30,640 jobs). San Francisco's tech employment fell 6% over the same period to 375,730 jobs. This is the first time in the report's 13-year history that NYC has surpassed SF. NYC's diversified job market and SF's announced layoffs drove the shift, though SF still ranks highest on overall talent pool depth across 13 metrics.
stories.impact: NYC's tech job growth (+30,640 jobs, 2022–2025) and SF's contraction signal major migration flow to Manhattan/Brooklyn, increasing white-collar renter demand in NYC core and spillover to outer boroughs, Westchester, and NJ transit corridors. Multifamily developers should prioritize NYC infill and transit-oriented sites in Queens, Brooklyn, and Hudson County over next 3–5 years; inbound tech talent will support above-market rent growth and unit absorption. Conversely, Bay Area multifamily faces headwinds; consider value-add repositioning over new supply.

stories.title: Principal Financial Group Loans $32M to Refi Queens Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: An affiliate of Mattone Investors secured $32 million to refinance Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot shopping center anchored by a Stop & Shop supermarket in the Queens neighborhood of Springfield Gardens. Principal Financial Group provided the debt, while Northmarq’s Robert Delitsky and Charles Cotsalas arranged the transaction. Delitsky noted in a statement that Mattone Investors first developed Springnex Plaza six years ago and “have done a fabulous job maintaining very strong occupancy” since then. “Supermarket-anchored shopping centers like Springnex Plaza will continue to attract very strong lender interest in today’s market,” Cotsalas added in the same statement. Located at 134-40 Springfield Boulevard, Springnex Plaza sits on 5.58 acres of land and is 100 percent occupied. Besides Stop & Shop, tenants include an IHOP, fashion retailer Ashley Stewart and Northwell Health GoHealth Urgent Care. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Principal Financial Group loaned $32M to refi Springnex Plaza, 96,028 SF supermarket-anchored center Queens.
Stop & Shop anchor + 100% occupancy at 5.58-acre Springfield Gardens site; Mattone Investors developer/owner.
Lender appetite strong for grocery-anchored retail despite office/retail sector weakness.
stories.summary: An affiliate of Mattone Investors secured a $32 million refinance from Principal Financial Group for Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot supermarket-anchored shopping center in Queens' Springfield Gardens neighborhood. The 5.58-acre property is 100% occupied and anchored by a Stop & Shop, with co-tenants including IHOP, Ashley Stewart, and Northwell Health GoHealth Urgent Care. Northmarq arranged the transaction.
stories.impact: Supermarket-anchored centers in outer-borough Queens remain lender-friendly despite retail distress; suggests strong neighborhood demand and resilience of essential-services retail. Limited relevance to multifamily directly, but outer-borough Queens strength (evidenced by full occupancy and easy refinancing) signals underlying residential demand. Multifamily developers should target mixed-use sites near grocery anchors in Queens and outer boroughs—built-in foot traffic supports smaller ground-floor retail and higher-density residential above.

stories.title: Data Center Development Has Domestic Materials Manufacturers Working Overtime
stories.excerpt: Development in the U.S. saw spotty progress in the first half of 2026 with costs of materials continuing to climb and asset classes with only the highest returns being built. That means data centers, power infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and pharmaceutical production are taking off, while office, retail and higher education on a national level lag way behind, due, in large part, to President Donald Trump’s ongoing tariff policies, according to a Skanska report. But just because there is a lull in some sectors does not mean supply chains for materials aren’t working at full capacity, Tom Park, vice president of national strategic supply chain at Skanska, told Commercial Observer. “The market is hot and cold right now — hot and warm may be a better way to say it — so what stands out is that we’re seeing a lot of project activity around data centers, semiconductor, life sciences,” Park said in an interview. “There’s really a lot of unprecedented demand in the mechanical, electrical, plumbing and steel space driving up lead times and cost.” Some factors causing these supply chain hemorrhages are Section 338 tariffs on Canada, delays on petrochemical import ships through the Strait of Hormuz, and domestic materials priced higher simply because of the supply and demand constraints. Tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper in particular are driving prices up. “What happens with tariffs is that it really raises the opportunity for domestic producers to raise their prices,” Park said. “For steel, aluminum and copper, the tariffs really have increased pricing on all those materials and derivative products because the foreign competition obviously has that tariff to overcome.” Lead times for material deliveries have increased from 24 to 36 weeks to 40 to 50 weeks, indicating to Park that metal mills and fabricators are running at full capacity. bullets: Data center, semiconductor, life sciences, advanced mfg. development accelerating; office/retail/higher ed lag.
Trump tariffs driving material cost inflation, lead time delays for steel, MEP goods.
Skanska reports 'unprecedented demand' in mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and steel for high-return projects.
stories.summary: According to a Skanska report, U.S. development in H1 2026 showed uneven progress, with data centers, semiconductors, life sciences, and advanced manufacturing booming while office, retail, and higher education lag. President Trump's tariff policies are driving material cost inflation and supply chain strain. Tom Park, Skanska VP of national strategic supply chain, noted 'unprecedented demand' in mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and steel, pushing lead times and costs higher for these sectors.
stories.impact: Tariff-driven MEP and steel cost inflation will compress multifamily development economics, especially for mid-to-high-rise buildings. Data center and life sciences demand is pulling labor and materials away from multifamily; expect construction labor scarcity and material cost growth through 2026–2027. Developers should lock in steel contracts and labor NOW; accelerate ground-up permitting for lower-rise, wood-frame product (lighter material load) in secondary markets. High-rise urban multifamily becomes less competitive vs. industrial/data center on marginal cost basis.

stories.title: Azora, Vizcaya Capital Flip Coconut Grove Office Building for $62M
stories.excerpt: Just a year after buying a boutique office building in Miami’s coveted Coconut Grove neighborhood, Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold it for a nearly $15 million gain. The five-story property at 3250 Mary Street, called the Grove at 3250 Mary, sold for $62.3 million, according to the brokers who represented the sellers, Berkadia’s Omar Morales and Jaret Turkell. The joint venture had purchased the 80,000-square-foot building for $47.5 million last September. Records show the buyer is an entity tied to El-Ad National Properties, the Boca Raton-based division of Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva’s El-Ad Group. “Coconut Grove continues to distinguish itself as one of South Florida’s strongest real estate markets, driven by exceptional demand from luxury residential buyers and high-net-worth office users,” Morales said in a statement. “That demand, combined with limited supply, continues to attract remarkable investment to the neighborhood.” In recent years, Coconut Grove has attracted a slew of billionaires, including Google’s billionaire founder Larry Page, who spent about $170 million assembling a residential compound last year. The residential acquisitions have fueled demand for luxury office space nearby. The acquisition of the 1982-built, 1.3-acre site office building marks somewhat of a deviation for El-Ad National, which has typically focused on residential and mixed-use development. It also comes just four months after the developer purchased a nearby, low-rise condo building for $45.5 million, which will likely be redeveloped. Earlier this month, up north in Fort Lauderdale, the firm bought an oceanfront hotel for $60 million. A representative for El-Ad Group was not immediately available for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialoserver.com.
bullets: Azora & Vizcaya Capital flipped Grove at 3250 Mary (Coconut Grove office) for $62.3M after 1-year hold.
Purchase price Sep 2025: $47.5M; sale price Aug 2026: $62.3M (+$14.8M gain, ~31% return).
Buyer: El-Ad National Properties (Israeli billionaire Tshuva's entity); strong HNW office demand in Coconut Grove.
stories.summary: Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold the Grove at 3250 Mary, an 80,000-square-foot five-story office building in Miami's Coconut Grove, for $62.3 million after holding for just one year. The joint venture had purchased the property for $47.5 million in September 2025, capturing a ~$14.8 million gain (31% return). Buyer is an entity tied to El-Ad National Properties, the U.S. division of Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva. Brokers cited strong demand from luxury residential buyers and high-net-worth office users in the neighborhood.
stories.impact: Coconut Grove office-to-residential conversion play is heating up; billionaire UHNW buyers recycling capital into trophy office assets in arbitrage play (office discount → residential/mixed-use upside). While this is office, not multifamily supply, it signals STRONG underlying residential demand and UHNW inflow to Miami/Coconut Grove. Developers should target office-to-residential conversion sites in Coconut Grove, Brickell, Wynwood before El-Ad and similar deep-pocketed players lock up inventory. Miami multifamily rents will follow office-to-residential pipeline over next 2–3 years.
